newsitem.title: PORTUGAL: Portugal yield curve to steepen - analysts.
newsitem.headline: Portugal yield curve to steepen - analysts.

text.p: Portugal's bond yield curve will steepen sharply this year as the Bank of Portugal pursues lower short-term interest rates at the same time as 10-year yields rise, analysts said.
Analysts believe that higher U.S. interest rates combined with robust German economic growth in 1998 will push up 10-year Bund yields, taking Portuguese yields with them.
The current 55-basis-point spread between German and Portuguese 10-year bonds is close to the minimum for the year and looks set to widen.
At the same time Portuguese short-end yields should fall since Portugal seems likely to meet the convergence criteria for Europe's single currency, allowing room for some easing of monetary policy.

"From now on 10-year bonds are dangerous. The Federal Reserve will have to raise interest rates by 50 basis points this year and again in 1998 and the German economy is going to grow steadily," said Nuno Godinho of Deutsche Morgan Grenfell.
He forecast a yield of 6.90 percent for the Portuguese 10-year bond (OT) at the end of this year compared to its current 6.45 percent.
"The Bundesbank will only raise rates from the first quarter of next year but 10-year bonds will anticipate this movement much earlier," he said.

According to a Reuters poll of eight analysts, 10-year OT yields are forecast to stand at an average 6.687 percent at the end of 1997. The minimum forecast was 6.40 percent and the maximum 6.90 percent.
The spread between 10-year OTs and Bunds hit an all-time minimum of 50 basis points last week, reflecting optimism that Spain and Portugal will join the "euro" from the start in 1999.

Analysts say the spread is now likely to widen until the decision on convergence is made in May, 1998. A Reuters poll of nine analysts, published today, forecast that Portugal would meet the Maastricht criteria this year.
If Portugal does qualify this would reduce the spread with Bunds again.

"At the end of 1998 the most likely scenario is for a clear reduction in the spread. I see long-term Bund rates at 6.30 percent and OTs at 6.50 percent," said Nuno Botelho at Banco Mello de Investimentos (BMI).
In the meantime analysts see short-term bond prices rising as the Bank of Portugal gradually cuts its rates to levels more in line with Germany.
Analysts see three-month rates at around 5.10 percent at the end of 1997, down from around 5.50 percent at present.
"Expectations of further rate cuts by the central bank persist and this will mean a steeper yield curve," said Jose Luis Alzola of Salomon Brothers.
The spread between March 1999 OTs and the February 2007 benchmark is 114 basis points. -- Lisbon editorial +(351-1) 3538254
